openMeasureModal:
Computes the horizontal distance, height difference and slope distance between two places from GPS.

  1. Stand at the first place and tap Save my current position for point A.
  2. Walk to the second place and save point B.
  3. The results are computed right away. The accuracy matches the phone's GPS (metres) — for short distances use a tape.
ar-metr:
A ruler projected into the camera image. You hold the phone flat, display up, so the rear camera looks straight down — the ground plane is then parallel to the sensor, there is no perspective in the image and the scale is the same across the whole picture. You see roughly 1.3 m at a holding height of 1 m and read to the centimetre.

  1. At the top enter the holding height in cm (or tap a preset 80 / 100 / 120). This is the only thing that changes in the field.
  2. Level the phone using the bubble level at the top right — until the bubble is green (within 0.7°) the values turn red.
  3. Scale projects a 10 cm grid and a cross with 1 cm ticks. Length = tap two points (you can drag them afterwards) and read the mm. Rectangle = two opposite corners, you get the sides and the area.
  4. Save writes the value into the job; under ⋯ → Records there is a list, CSV export and a To point button (it goes into the point's note, so it is also in the backup and the exports).

First a one-off calibration, otherwise it lies. The app does not know your phone's camera field of view and without calibration it assumes 66° — which can be off by tens of percent. Put a tape measure or an A4 sheet (long side 297 mm) on the ground, switch to Length, tap both ends and enter the real length under ⋯ → Calibrate. The calibration is stored separately for each camera resolution. If you do not know the holding height, turn it around — the Fine-tune holding height button computes it instead.

Limits you have to live with: an error in the entered height passes through 1:1 (5 cm out of a metre = 5 % on all values), 1° of tilt makes ~1 cm per metre at the edge of the view, and the lens distorts at the edges of the image — the tool warns you, so measure through the centre. Realistically achievable is ±1 %, i.e. ±1 cm per metre. It cannot see further than the width of the view and it does not work at an angle: the error would grow as h/sin²(angle below the horizon), at three metres already ~15 cm per 1° of tilt. It measures the horizontal projection — on a sloping surface enter ⋯ → Surface slope and the length along the slope is added. It is not for acceptance or invoicing, but for a quick "how wide is that joint" it is.
startAreaMode:
Area and perimeter of a polygon in the S-JTSK plane (Gauss formula) — an exact computation for Czechia.

  1. Tap the map to add a vertex, or walk around the plot and add My point (uses the averaged GPS).
  2. The panel at the bottom shows the area, perimeter and number of vertices live.
  3. Undo removes the last vertex. Finish closes the mode — if you tap it by mistake, a toast offers Undo and the walked polygon comes back.

The accuracy is set by the GPS: an area walked with a phone is an estimate within a few percent, not a basis for a cadastral area. Compute an exact area with the Parcel tool from surveyed boundary corners.
openCheckDist:
A check of the survey geometry: it compares a length you measured with a tape against the length computed from the S-JTSK coordinates of both points. It shows whether the survey holds together or whether there is an error somewhere.

  1. Choose a pair of points from the job.
  2. Enter the measured length for it (tape, rangefinder, a value from a survey plan or sketch).
  3. The deviation is shown in mm and ppm; an exceeded tolerance is highlighted.

The average deviation over all pairs is the systematic part — when all measures pull in the same direction, it is not a random error but a scale or wrong units.
openDmtVolume:
A digital terrain model from points with a height: a Delaunay triangulated network (TIN), from it contour lines and volumes of cut and fill against a reference plane.

  1. The points of the job that have a height (Z / Bpv) are taken. Data from a total station or RTK can also be pasted manually as rows of Y X Z.
  2. Enter the reference height — you get the volume of cut, fill and the area.
  3. You set the contour interval; the model is drawn on its own canvas, it does not touch the main map or AR.

The accuracy stands and falls with the points: the TIN interpolates only between them, computes nothing outside the hull of the points, and the break lines of the terrain need to be surveyed.
vyska-objektu:
Trigonometric determination of the height of a mast, chimney, tree… with the phone alone: you sight the vertical angle to the foot and to the top of the object, the height is computed.

  1. Enter the height of the phone above the ground (where you aim from — roughly eye height).
  2. The distance to the object is computed from the sight to the foot (assumes level ground) — or measure it with a tape/by pacing and enter it manually, that is more accurate.
  3. Aim the cross at the foot of the object and tap "Sight the foot", then at the top and "Sight the top".

The result also shows an honest ± estimate (typically decimetres up to ~1 m). You improve it by going closer, holding the phone steady, or entering the distance manually.
korekce:
Three corrections that are computed in the field all the time — with temperature, pressure and humidity pre-filled from the last downloaded weather (and overwritable by hand).

  1. Tape: thermal expansion, comparison correction, sag and conversion of the slope length to horizontal; the breakdown of the corrections is in mm.
  2. Rangefinder ppm: the EDM atmospheric correction you enter into the total station, including how many mm it makes over 100 m and 1 km. Check the reference atmosphere of your instrument in the manual.
  3. Refraction: the correction of the trigonometric height difference (1−k)·d²/2R with an adjustable coefficient.

The pressure from the weather is at sea level, the rangefinder needs the pressure at the site — the conversion from the GPS height is shown above the inputs. A measured thermometer and barometer always take precedence over the forecast; the temperature of a tape on hot asphalt is different from the air temperature.
obchuzka:
A volume on the spot, without office processing: you walk around the edge of the excavation, survey the bottom and know the volume right away — with an honest ± too.

  1. Walk around the edge starts automatic recording (a vertex every 1.5 m, bad fixes are discarded). Stop at the corners and use Corner manually — it averages for a few seconds, the corner is the most important place of the perimeter.
  2. Bottom: best is to walk around the edge of the bottom as well (≥ 3 points) — the volume is then computed as a truncated pyramid and the battered walls are included. 1–2 bottom points are enough too, or a depth entered manually (tape, staff) — that is more accurate than the height from GPS.
  3. At the top are the volume, area (Gauss formula in S-JTSK), perimeter and depth; next to the volume a ± computed from the accuracy of the fixes.
  4. Transfer the points into the job saves them as points with the code "excavation edge" / "excavation bottom"; Into the volumes (TIN) hands them straight to the Volumes/contour lines tool. Export CSV pulls out the coordinates and the results.

Vertical walls are an upper estimate — without a surveyed bottom the volume comes out larger than it really is; the app says so next to the result. Everything rests on the phone's GPS and its height is 2–3× worse than the position, so the main error comes from the depth: for a small excavation the ± may be tens of percent. For acceptance and invoicing a rover or a total station belongs there. This tool is not a 3D scan or photogrammetry — a model of the excavation from a video cannot be computed in a browser.
presne-mereni:
In short: a phone has three GPS errors and each is dealt with differently. Noise (every fix somewhere else, ±3–5 m) is reduced by long averaging — Precise GPS. Offset (all fixes in the same direction, 1–3 m) averaging does not see; only a comparison with something known reveals it — an edge from the map (Calibration by walking), a known point (GPS shift to a known point) or a second phone (DGPS). Drift (the offset changes by 0.5–1 m within 20 min) is handled by calibrating before and after the measurement with a recomputation of the points by time.

  1. Calibration by walking along an edge: on the orthophoto tap out a sharp edge (a kerb, the outline of a plot — Close shape), walk it there and back, switch the correction on.
  2. Precise GPS: the centre of the phone on the point, 10–15 min, turn by 90° when told, save.
  3. Walk the edge again: the app offers to recompute the points measured in between.
  4. A second phone: offer the saved point as a temporary DGPS base, or measure distances from it with the acoustic rangefinder (the shape to the cm).

What to expect horizontally: bare GPS ±3–5 m → Precise GPS ±0.5–1 m → with calibration by walking ±0.3–0.5 m → with walking before and after ±0.3–0.4 m; DGPS rover ±0.5 m relative to the base; acoustics ±2–5 cm relative to known points. Height always ±1–2 m. It is not RTK — a phone does not give raw satellite measurements. The window has a procedure for each method, a table "where calibration works and where it does not" and typical situations (paving, a plot, a field without a point).
brutal-gps:
In short: the phone lies on the point, the app averages hundreds of fixes, throws out jumps and at each quarter asks you to turn the phone by 90° — that cancels out where exactly its antenna is. It reduces the GPS noise; the GPS offset it does not know by itself, that it takes from the Calibration by walking along an edge or the Shift to a known point, when switched on.

  1. Check the Site score row at the top — red = find a better place or time.
  2. Where to put the phone: over the point goes the centre of the phone (the cross in the picture in the window), display up, away from your body and metal. The GPS antenna is near the top edge (5–7 cm from the centre, in a different place on every model) — that is why you turn around the centre, not the antenna.
  3. Choose the duration: 10–15 min is the optimum (5 min ≈ ±0.7 m, 15 min ≈ ±0.4–0.5 m; 30 min adds almost nothing unless you calibrate by walking before and after). Start; at ¼, ½ and ¾ of the time the app asks you to turn the phone by 90° clockwise.
  4. Save the result as a point — the achieved accuracy stays with it, as does which correction was added. Or add it as a session and come back later ("When to come back?" advises a time) — a combined result from several sessions is more accurate.
  5. After saving the app offers the point as a temporary DGPS base for a second phone; and if calibration by walking was on, walk the edge again — the point is recomputed by the time of measurement.

For maximum accuracy plan the campaign "3 visits" with the card below: measuring in three different satellite constellations cancels a large part of the systematic error. What to expect: ±0.5–1 m alone, ±0.3–0.5 m with calibration by walking; height ±1–2 m.
rajon:
The classic polar method: a new point from a station (a known point) using a direction and a horizontal distance.

  1. Choose the station and the orientation (another known point), or use the compass.
  2. Enter the direction/bearing and the distance (tape, rangefinder).
  3. The point is computed and saved into the job with a note on its origin.
offset-point:
A point you cannot reach or stand on: a building corner, the centre of a manhole, the foot of a pole, a point behind a fence. It is computed from a base + azimuth + horizontal distance.

  1. Choose the base: my position (averaged GPS), or one of the saved points.
  2. Enter the azimuth — either as a number, or take it from the compass (aim the phone at the target and tap).
  3. Enter the horizontal distance (tape, rangefinder) and save the point.

The azimuth is geographic (0° = north, clockwise), like everywhere else in the app. The accuracy is set by the accuracy of the base and the compass — near buildings and metal the compass is unreliable, then rather use the Radial point from a point with a known orientation.
ar-intersection:
Determining an unknown point by sights from two (or more) known stations — purely from angles, without measuring a distance.

  1. Stand on a known point, aim at the point you are looking for and save the sight.
  2. The same from a second known point.
  3. The app intersects the directions (more sights are adjusted by least squares) and saves the point.
pdr-offset:
A new point "by pacing": from a known point A you walk to place B and the app computes B = A + a vector from the steps (accelerometer) and the direction (compass). Over 10–30 m it tends to be more accurate than two separate GPS measurements — ideal for building corners and places without a view of the sky.

  1. Once in a while do a step calibration: a straight section ≥ 25 m under open sky with a good fix.
  2. Stand on point A, choose it in the list and start walking.
  3. Hold the phone loosely in front of you, display up, and walk normally to B; stop, name the point and save it.

Near buildings metal disturbs the compass — so an honest uncertainty estimate is saved with the point (~2 % of the distance ⊕ the direction error). For longer distances use the Offset point with a tape.
ar-resection:
Determining your own position and north from sights to known points (like a free station) — it helps where the GPS is not enough.

  1. Aim one by one at 2–3 known points in the field.
  2. The app computes where you stand and aligns north in AR.
free-station:
A guide to determining your own station from sights to known points — when you are not standing on any known point and the GPS is not enough.

  1. Choose 2–3 known points you can see from the place.
  2. The guide takes you through the sights (it delegates to the AR resection).
  3. The result is your position + aligned north in AR.
dgps:
In short: two phones at the same moment are wrong by almost the same amount. Leave one lying on a point where you know where it is (the base) — it measures how much the GPS is off right now; with the other you measure (the rover) and the app subtracts that error. Typically to a half or a third of the error. Two ways: live over the internet (new points are corrected right when saved) or QR / file (offline, corrected retrospectively).

  1. Base: put phone A on a point with reliably known coordinates (an official point, an S-JTSK import). If you have none, first measure one with Precise GPS with calibration by walking — Precise GPS offers it right after saving as a temporary base. Start it and leave it lying for the WHOLE time of measuring.
  2. Live: on the base tap Share corrections live — a six-character code appears. On the rover open Live from the internet, copy the code and Connect to the base. From then on the current correction is added to the points you save (also in Precise GPS); a "DGPS live" pill is lit at the top and the app tells you when the base has not sent for 3 min or when you are further than 2 km. Disconnect switches the correction off and offers a retrospective correction of the points saved before connecting.
  3. QR / file: measure normally with the rover; then on the base Stop and show the QR with the corrections, on the rover Corrections from QR → Scan the QR from the base (or a file). Check the offered shifts and confirm.

What to expect: the rover's points relative to each other ±0.5 m (best within 150 m of the base, valid up to ~2–3 km). The position of the whole is as good as you know the base point: an official point ±0.5 m, a point from Precise GPS with calibration ±0.6–1 m (its error passes to all rover points as a common shift — the shape and distances stay), a GPS point without calibration = only the shape, the whole may be shifted by metres. A temporary base also extends the validity of the calibration by walking in time (the 20 min limit falls away). The live mode needs the internet on both phones (~4 kB per minute); the base code is the only secret, valid for a day. Retrospectively only the points measured while the base was running and without a correction already added get corrected; the shift is written into the journal and applied at most once.

Quality of the correction (since 16 Sep 2026): the base block is the median of the fixes weighted by the reported accuracy (one reflection off a wall no longer shifts a whole minute), the rover weights fresh blocks more than three-minute-old ones and discards a block out of line. It cannot reach centimetres: only the error common to both phones (atmosphere, satellite orbits) is subtracted; reflections, noise and position smoothing are each phone's own. What helps most is a base with an open horizon, the same type of phone and the rover within 150 m.
akusticky-dalkomer:
The distance between two phones from sound, to the centimetre — no other hardware. The phone on a known point replies with a beep, the other measures: each finds in its own recording when it beeped and when the other one did (one sample = 7 mm of sound path), and the clock difference cancels out by itself. A distance to a known point is classic surveying, only the rangefinder is sound; two distances to two known points give a new point by intersection — without GPS.

  1. The first time do the Zero calibration (2.00 m): the phones with their bottom edges facing each other exactly 2.00 m apart by tape, the second one has I am standing on a known point switched on.
  2. Put phone B with its bottom edge on the known point and switch on I am standing on a known point. It only listens and replies.
  3. Hold phone A with its bottom edge above the place being measured, switch on Measuring (this phone) and tap Measure. You will hear a beep and two replies; in a few seconds you have the distance (3 rounds, the median is taken).
  4. Save the distance to the known point. Move B to the second known point, measure again and under Distances to known points tick both → Point from two distances. Choose the intersection you are standing at and save the point.

Enter the air temperature (10 °C = 2 % of the distance; it is taken from the Weather when known). It works up to ~40 m outdoors, the phones must "see" each other; wind and machine noise in the chirp band worsen the accuracy. On an iPhone switch off the silent mode and allow the microphone. Both the microphone and the speaker are at the bottom edge — that is the measuring mark (±3 cm). The best intersection angle is 60–120°.
kalibrace-hranou:
In short: the GPS in a phone is off by a few metres, but for a while in the same direction. When you walk a piece of an edge the app knows from the map, it works out by how much and where the GPS is off right now — and subtracts that from the points you save afterwards. The same correction as "GPS shift to a known point", but without stopping and without a known point.

  1. On the map switch to the orthophoto and find a sharp edge on the ground: a kerb, the edge of asphalt, the foot of a wall, a manhole cover. A street map is unsuitable (freehand lines, ±1–5 m), roofs too (they are displaced in the photo). A tap within 4 m of a parcel boundary snaps to it: with the Cadastre layer on the app downloads the parcel outline from RÚIAN itself (the nearest place on the boundary, not just a corner), without a signal it takes the parcels saved in the job. You cannot see the boundary in the field — walk along it only where something marks it (a boundary stone, a kerb, a fence — which often does not sit on it). In an area with UKM (a redrawn analogue map) the boundary is only accurate to metres, the app counts ±1 m.
  2. Choose on the map: tap the start, the bends and the end of the edge you will really walk along, then Done. For a plot, a plus sign or a square tap Close shape (or tap back to the first point): on a straight line only the component perpendicular to it comes out, on a bent or closed line the whole vector. Or choose two saved points.
  3. Lateral offset: if you walk 0.4 m to the right of the tapped edge, enter +0.4 (left negative).
  4. Start walking along the line and walk steadily from the green end to the red one, the phone loosely in your hand, best there and back (the app then separates how far you hold the phone to the side). 30–50 m is enough. At the bottom you see how many fixes there are already and by how much the GPS is off so far.
  5. Stop and compute → Switch on the correction. It is added to newly saved points (also in Precise GPS), watched for 20 min and 300 m from the place of walking: a pill at the top says "GPS correction · X min left · Y m from the place" and the app warns 5 min before expiry, on expiry, at 200 m and at 300 m.
  6. Calibration before and after: when you have finished measuring, walk the edge again (within 90 min, within 500 m). The app shows by how much the GPS error shifted in between and offers to recompute by time the points saved between the two walks (a point in the middle gets half of the difference). The vector is replaced, not added; the changes go into the journal.

What to expect: 30–50 m of walking with fixes ±3–5 m gives ±0.3–0.5 m, with a good signal and a longer walk ±0.2 m — plus the accuracy of the line (orthophoto ±0.2–0.5 m, cadastral boundary ±0.14–0.3 m, saved points ±cm), which the app adds and shows as "total". Next to the result you also see the drift of the error during the walk (first vs. second half, for a closed shape the same as the closure): above 1 m it is a restless day, calibrate more often and measure right after walking. The correction applies to the points being saved, not to the live position in navigation. The expandable text "How it works" in the window explains the principle and the computation.
openStakeoutModal:
Ticking off staked-out points: walk to the point, drive the stake, tap done. The overview of what is left survives closing the app — the state is kept per job.

  1. Tap a point in the list — the app highlights it and navigates to it (arrow in AR).
  2. After driving the stake, tick the point off; the time and GPS accuracy at that moment are stored.
  3. The Only my own points switch hides official points so they don't clutter the list.
  4. Export the stake-out report (CSV) pulls out the list with times for the office.

The tick is bound to the point, not to its position — if you delete the point and create it again, it starts unticked.
stakeout-line:
For linear works (road, kerb, fence, trench): you enter an axis — two points give a straight line, more points a polyline — and while you walk the app shows where on it you are.

  1. Pick the axis points in order from the start. Add another vertex with Add vertex, remove it with the cross.
  2. While walking you read the chainage (how far you are from the start along the axis, across vertices), the perpendicular offset (how far left or right you are), which segment you stand on, how much is left to the vertex and to the end.
  3. Start chainage aligns the numbers with the design: if the section starts at km 1.200, enter 1200 and the app counts 1200…1400 instead of 0…200. The same numbers go to the camera and to the collapsed strip.
  4. The other way round it can stake out a point at a given chainage (optionally with a perpendicular offset) and save it as a job point.
  5. Stake out the whole axis by metres drops stakes at a regular step (every 10, 25, 50 m) along the whole section including the end — named by chainage (ST1225), so the stake-out checklist ticks them off directly.

It is computed in a plane around the first vertex — fine for axes kilometres long. The perpendicular offset is only as accurate as your GPS, so for centimetre work use a tape from the staked points. At a sharp vertex the offset point lies on the perpendicular of the segment the chainage belongs to (like with a total station), not on the angle bisector.
vrstvy:
Pavement structures per site/section: layers from top to bottom with thickness and % compaction surcharge. Add layers from the catalogue (ACO, ACL, ACP, SMA, MZK, ŠD…) or your own; the glossary at the bottom explains the abbreviations.

  1. Choose which layer the model in the machine controller corresponds to (top surface).
  2. Choose which layer you are laying.
  3. At the top the value Into the tablet lights up = offset between layers + compaction surcharge.

In the cross-section you change thickness by dragging the line between layers; the crossfall (one-sided or crowned) is only a preview, exaggerated. The default compaction % is indicative — adjust it after the compaction trial.
indoor:
In a hall, a car park or a tunnel GPS ends. This tool keeps the position going: from a point you know it computes your displacement and shows distance and direction to job points — on your own floor plan, because the map would show the roof indoors.

  1. Choose where you start from — the point you stand on (best), or the last GPS at the entrance.
  2. Start tracking the position. On Android the app tries visual tracking (WebXR) from the camera and sensors; where that is missing (iPhone), steps are counted from the accelerometer and the direction from the compass.
  3. The uncertainty is always shown at the top and as a circle in the floor plan. It grows with the distance walked.
  4. As soon as you reach a surveyed point, select it and tap I am on the point — the position is aligned, the uncertainty drops to zero and the app shows how much drift had accumulated until then. That number tells you how often you need to re-tie.

This is not stake-out. The uncertainty doesn't drop below decimetres and after fifty metres of walking it is metres — partitions, penetrations and openings belong to a total station or a laser. Indoors the compass also goes haywire (metal, switchboards, lifts), so the step-based computation drifts more than outside. The step length is calibrated outdoors in the Step offset tool (shared value). The app doesn't read IFC/BIM — load the floor plan as DXF with the Project import tool and transfer the vertices to the job.
openTachymetrie:
A digital replacement for the hand-drawn field sketch: points are drawn at their correct position over the chosen background (map, orthophoto, or none), joined by lines of various types and can be labelled.

  1. Add points from your position, or pull in the job points with the My points button.
  2. Join them with lines, insert texts (e.g. "stone" inside an area); lengths are computed for lines and area for closed shapes.
  3. Export to PNG asks whether you want a clean sketch on white (for the report) or the sketch with the background map (to document where it is).

There can be several sketches. On the left of the bar is a drop-down with sketches and next to it + (new), pencil (rename) and bin (delete this sketch with its content). Switching loses nothing — each sketch is saved separately on the phone.
zapisnik:
A digital field book instead of paper: technical levelling (backsight/foresight readings → height differences, heights, misclosure) and horizontal directions — for each target sets with Hz in face I/II (reduction + means), zenith angles in both faces (averaged) and a slope or horizontal distance (slope with zenith is converted to horizontal and height difference).

The computations run continuously (can be switched off in the field book header). Data is stored per job and can be exported.
zavady:
Record a finding in the field in a few taps: photo → category → severity → note. Position, time and GPS accuracy fill in by themselves. A defect can be tied to a specific measured point ("which point and what's wrong with it") — the position is then taken from the point and its name appears in the list, CSV and report.

  1. Open the tool (or hold the "New point" button in the dock) and fill in the form.
  2. Defects show as coloured exclamation marks in the map and AR — by severity.
  3. In the list tick them as Resolved; nothing is lost.

Export: CSV with S-JTSK coordinates and a printable report with photos (save as PDF).
hlasovky:
Dictated notes that are transcribed to text right away — you can't type in gloves and mud, and plain audio would have to be played back in the office. Every note gets a geo-stamp: time, position (S-JTSK), GPS accuracy and the nearest own point within 25 m ("at point 105, 3 m").

  1. Tap Record a note and speak — the text appears live under the button. Another tap stops it (5-minute cap).
  2. Check and correct the transcript in the list — recognition mangles mainly names and jargon (S-JTSK, Bpv, ZPMZ the app fixes itself). The audio stays saved as evidence.
  3. If the transcript is missing, tap Dictate and dictate the text afterwards, or type it.
  4. With many notes, search them with the field at the top. In the evening the Day journal collects them, text included.

Transcription may be unavailable: on iPhone (and in the PWA) the browser often can't do it at all — the window says so right under the button and the note is saved as audio, recording carries on. Transcription also needs signal (the browser sends the audio to the vendor's server) — offline only audio is saved and you add the text later. Transcription can be switched off in the header; on iOS try that if the microphone makes the AR camera image stutter. Data stays on the phone only (no cloud, not in the job export).
denik-dne:
An evening summary of the day for the active job in one tap — material for the office or the site diary: new/changed/deleted points, crew attendance, defects including status, weather, walked track and created field books.

  1. Open the tile — the summary for today builds itself; at the top switch to yesterday or any date.
  2. Share sends a plain text report (mail, WhatsApp…); where sharing is unavailable it is copied to the clipboard.
  3. Save PDF opens a printable report — save it via the system print (allow pop-ups).

It only reads data from this device: attendance clocked on another phone isn't here and old points without a timestamp can't be assigned to a day. Works offline (weather shows the last downloaded data for the chosen day).
track-log:
Recording the walked route (GPS track) into the map: walking a boundary, surveying a path. The track can be saved and exported (GPX/KML).

  1. Tap Start recording — the track is drawn in orange on the map, a point is taken after moving ≥ 1.5 m (saves GPS noise and battery).
  2. Tick Show the track in AR too to see the line laid on the ground in the camera as well — handy when you go back along your own track.
  3. Export GPX saves the route for Kokeš, QGIS or maps.
geo-foto:
A photo that still shows where and when it was taken even after forwarding by mail or WhatsApp: the stamp is burned straight into the pixels — job, S-JTSK, Bpv height, date and time, viewing azimuth and GPS accuracy. EXIF gets discarded when forwarding, a burned-in stamp does not.

  1. Tap Take a stamped photo — the viewfinder opens and at the top you see live what will be burned into the photo (if azimuth or fix is missing, it says so before you press the shutter).
  2. In the line at the bottom you can add a short note that will be part of the stamp.
  3. A photo within 25 m of your point ties itself to it; the To point button attaches it to the point card.
  4. Save PDF makes a report for the day or the whole job — photos, coordinates, hashes.

What the stamp doesn't prove: burned-in pixels can be repainted in an editor. That is why a SHA-256 hash is computed for each photo and stored with the hash of the previous one — the Verify chain button checks offline that the set wasn't swapped or reordered after capture. It is not an electronic signature under eIDAS. If the camera doesn't work (permission denied), the system app takes the photo and no azimuth is stored — a made-up direction would be worse than an honest "undetermined". Photos are only on this phone.
epochy:
Watching whether a point moves over time (displacement monitoring): bridge cornice, retaining wall, landslide, landfill… You measure the same point repeatedly with a total station or a GNSS rover and after each measurement enter the resulting coordinates here as a new "epoch".

  1. Create a monitored point — new, or choose an existing one from your own points.
  2. After each measurement add an epoch: enter Y/X/Z by hand, photograph the display or report (OCR reads them), or take them from a point in the app.
  3. The first epoch is the reference — the horizontal displacement ΔP and vertical ΔZ of all further epochs are computed against it.

Optionally set limit deviations in mm — when exceeded the point turns red. A chart shows the displacement trend, everything can be exported to CSV. The phone's GPS is only an emergency option (±metres, not enough for real monitoring).

In the detail of a monitored point you can set a re-measurement reminder (every 7/14/30 days or a custom interval). After start the app warns with a bar about overdue points (counted from the last epoch) and a red dot with a count lights up on the tool tile; system notifications can optionally be enabled too.
kvalita-bodu:
A table of all job points with what they were measured by and how well. The app computed the spread before, but only one number of it reached the point — here is the full record: "the point is from 240 readings, spread σ 0.42 m" can be backed up, "±0.3 m" is just a claim.

  1. Open the tile — points are sorted from the newest.
  2. The ± error column is the standard error of the resulting position, σ the spread of the individual readings around the centre, epochs how many readings were used (and how many arrived in total).
  3. Report (.txt) saves a readable list for the job, Table (.csv) opens in Excel.

Only points that came from GPS have a spread — for hand-entered Y/X there is a dash because they have no readings and a number would lie. The most data is carried by points from Precise GPS (long averaging); it also records the epoch count across all re-occupation sessions.

What it doesn't say: the values only describe the internal agreement of the phone's measurement. A systematic error (signal reflections off façades, troposphere) is not removed by averaging — that is why the ± error is bounded from below by a realistic limit. It doesn't replace a check measurement by an independent method.
kos:
Deleted jobs and own points aren't thrown away immediately: they lie in the bin for 30 days and can be restored. The "Undo" toast disappears in a few seconds, this stays — a job deleted by mistake in the field is therefore not a final loss.

  1. Open the bin and find the item by deletion time.
  2. Restore brings it back including connections and settings.

It holds the 15 latest records and after 30 days they are discarded by themselves. Downloaded official points aren't put in the bin — they are big and can be downloaded again from ČÚZK any time. The bin lives only on this phone, so it doesn't replace a backup.
usadit-ar:
One entry instead of seven calibration tools: the guide asks what bothers you (rotated markers / offset / I don't know where I stand / seat the job) and starts the right tool itself.

The hidden calibration tiles are still reachable via search.
kompas:
A classic rose with both norths at once: the white tip is true (geographic) north, which the app uses for all azimuths, the red needle is magnetic north, which a hand compass shows. The green line at the top is fixed — below it you read where the phone is pointing right now.

  1. Hold the phone flat and away from metal (car, fence, rebar, switchboard) — the magnetometer is the weakest link of AR and near metal it can be off by tens of degrees.
  2. Next to the rose both azimuths are written as numbers and below them the declination at your place (computed from the position, positive = east).
  3. When the compass misbehaves, go through "How to calibrate the compass" (figure-eight with the phone) or verify it with the by the Sun button.
  4. The same window also has the user zero (changes only the displayed number), North alignment (shifts AR and the map) and the degrees / gons switch.

Don't mix the two in one computation: in Czechia the declination is about 5° east, which over 100 m is almost 9 m of shift. Azimuths from the app, from the cadastre and from coordinates are true; the magnetic value is here for comparison with a hand compass and for older sketches. On a computer without a sensor the rose stays at "waiting…".
agOpenCalibrate:
Calibrating AR north by a known point: you aim at a point in the field and the app trims the compass rotation so that AR fits.

  1. Pick a point in the map/AR that you can clearly see in the field.
  2. Aim the centre of the screen at it and confirm.
  3. The north correction is stored (cancel it in the Compass).
ar-calib2:
More precise AR calibration by two known points: the app aligns rotation (north) and shift so that both points in AR fit reality.

  1. Pick the first point you can clearly see in the field, aim the centre of the screen at it and confirm.
  2. Same with the second point — ideally in a different direction (not in line).
  3. The correction is stored; cancel it with a new calibration or in the Compass.

Unlike "Align north" (1 point) it also solves the position shift — useful when GPS "pulls" sideways.
orient-point:
Quick trimming of AR north by a point you can see in the field — the magnetic compass is the weakest link of AR and near cars, fences and power lines it can be off by tens of degrees.

  1. Pick a known point visible from here (trig point, control point, a corner surveyed earlier).
  2. Aim the centre of the screen at it and confirm.
  3. The app compares the true azimuth to the point with what the compass reports and stores the difference as the north correction.

The correction is the same lever as "North alignment" in the Compass — you reset it there too. The farther the target point, the more precise the alignment. This is the simpler variant of "Align north"; the position shift is handled only by "Align AR on 2 points".
localization-helmert:
Seating the survey on known points with a Helmert transformation: from pairs of identical points (my measurement ↔ given coordinates) it computes shift, rotation and scale and applies them to the job.

  1. Match at least 2 identical points (more = check, least-squares adjustment).
  2. Check the deviations at the individual points (residuals).
  3. Confirm — the transformation is applied; it can be undone.
ref-calibration:
Correcting the systematic GPS shift by a known point. You stand on a point with reliable coordinates, the app compares where GPS reports it and remembers the difference as a constant shift.

  1. Stand on a known point and let GPS settle (the longer the averaging, the better).
  2. Enter its coordinates — S-JTSK Y/X, or pick it from the list (ČÚZK control points including levelling ones, and your own points). Faster: in the point card tap the little Correct GPS square.
  3. Height: if the point has a Bpv height (levelling benchmark, many trig and densification points), the vertical shift is computed too — put the phone on the mark, or in the "Phone above the mark" field write how much higher you hold it. A levelling benchmark gives the height to millimetres; its position in ČÚZK is only to a metre, but that's still better than the phone.
  4. Confirm the shift. From then on it is added to newly saved points (position and height from the GPS average; a height overwritten from the DEM doesn't change) until you switch the correction off.

Where you stand decides: under a tree, by a wall or between houses the signal reflects and GPS has a different error there than 30 m away in the open — a correction from such a place is valid only for the same conditions and in the open may shift wrongly. The app recognises that from the spread of the average and the reported accuracy and warns; better pick a point with a clear horizon and let GPS average for 1–2 minutes. Gravity points aren't offered (they tend to be inside buildings, position only approximate).

Mind two things: the shift is applied to newly created points, not to the displayed position and not retroactively to points already saved (those stay unchanged). And it is valid only over a small area (hundreds of metres) and a short time — it is a local correction, not RTK; the vertical GPS error changes even faster than the horizontal, so take the height with reserve and calibrate more often. Another way is Two-phone DGPS, or — when you can't stand on the point but an edge is visible in the orthophoto — Calibration by walking along an edge.
fov-kalib:
Measures the real field of view of your phone's camera. AR uses it to compute where on the screen to draw a marker — if it is set wrong, points in the middle of the image fit but drift apart towards the edges. Every phone model has a different one; guessing it with a slider is a lottery.

  1. Go outside, calibrate the compass (figure-eight with the phone) and pick a distant isolated object — a mast, a chimney, a house corner. It must be farther than ~50 m, otherwise your own movement gets into the measurement.
  2. Turn the phone so the object lies exactly at the left edge of the image and tap Record. Then so it is at the right edge and record again — the azimuth difference is the horizontal field of view.
  3. This is repeated 3× and the middle value is taken; the compass wobbles, so one measurement isn't enough. A spread above 6° means "measure again".
  4. The vertical angle you either measure the same way (a tall object at the top and bottom edge, the phone's tilt is tracked) or let it be computed from the image aspect ratio.
  5. Finally Save to settings.

When the compass misbehaves, the wall method is described inside too: at a known distance D you measure the width W between the image edges and FOV = 2·arctan(W/2D). Check after saving: a point you can see in the field must fit in AR at the edge of the screen too, not just in the middle.
ar-visual-track:
Anchors the AR image with the camera (optical flow): markers shake less and don't float when the phone moves.

Switch it on here or in Settings → AR camera. It costs some extra battery — switch off when you need to save it. Beta: if AR "drifts away", switch it off and report when it happened.
gps-semafor:
A green / amber / red traffic light before measuring: it combines satellite geometry (PDOP), your elevation mask from Signal prediction, the accuracy reported by the phone and the surroundings.

  1. Choose what is around you: open sky / trees or one wall / between buildings.
  2. Read the verdict and tips — e.g. "move away from the wall" or in how many minutes the constellation will be better (it searches up to 2 h ahead).

Reflections off façades and cars (multipath) cause errors of metres that averaging does NOT remove — prevention works better than long measurement. You also see the score directly in Brutal GPS.
openSatModal:
Overview of satellites (GPS, Galileo, GLONASS, BeiDou) above the horizon: how many there are, where in the sky and what the geometry is.

Few satellites low above the horizon = worse accuracy. Use it before a more precise measurement — wait for a better constellation.
sky-obstruction:
Skyplot for the current position and time: with the slider you set the elevation mask (how much of the sky is blocked by houses, trees, a slope) and the app shows how many satellites remain above the mask and how good the geometry will be (PDOP).

Useful for planning measurements in built-up areas or by a forest.
gnss-forecast:
A forecast of GPS measuring conditions 24 hours ahead — like a weather forecast, but for satellites. It tells you when to do the most precise points today and when to postpone.

  1. Open the tile; the app computes the hourly PDOP (satellite geometry) from their orbits and adds the Kp index (ionosphere state from NOAA).
  2. Green dot = excellent conditions, yellow = usable, red = weak geometry or a geomagnetic storm.
  3. At the top is the best window — plan stake-out, a check or Brutal GPS for it.

Satellite orbits (TLE) and Kp are downloaded from the internet, then they work offline from cache for days. The forecast is for an open horizon — shading by trees and houses is judged by the "Signal prediction" tool. The storm note is a safety one, unrelated to GNSS accuracy.
pocasi:
A forecast for the measuring site blended from up to 33 sources — 19 forecast models (ECMWF incl. the AI models AIFS/GraphCast, DWD ICON, ČHMÚ ALADIN at 1 km resolution, KNMI and DMI HARMONIE, GeoSphere AROME, Météo-France, UK Met Office, NOAA, JMA, CMA, BOM, CMC), MET Norway, DWD MOSMIX, 11 ensembles (incl. Google WeatherNext 2 with 64 runs) and, in Czechia, also measured data from ČHMÚ. All values are averaged with weights — the Source agreement tile shows how much the models disagree; a large spread = an uncertain forecast. The app also knows how well each model did over the last month (it pulls the history from the archive right away, no waiting) and gives the better ones more weight — details in the expandable row "What the forecast is based on" at the very bottom.

ČHMÚ ALADIN is the model the Czech hydrometeorological institute computes its forecasts with, and with a 1 km step it is the finest of the whole mix (ICON-D2 has 2.2 km). For Czechia it therefore has one of the highest short-range weights. It computes three days ahead, then global models take over.

Weights are computed as in a survey adjustment: 1/σ² from the actually measured error of the source — a source twice as accurate gets four times the weight, not a third more. Outlying sources are also excluded: when one model claims something five degrees off from all the others, it doesn't enter the result at all (it is struck through in the source list). This is found via median and MAD, not mean and standard deviation — the outlier would hide itself in those. For precipitation nothing is excluded; a heavy shower would look like an outlier even though it's true. Where the app knows a model's systematic error, it subtracts it right away: a model that is consistently a degree too warm at this place gets corrected, not just down-weighted.

An ensemble is the average of all runs of one model (ECMWF 51 runs, ICON-D2 twenty) — it tends to be more accurate than a single run because random errors cancel out. For Czechia the most valuable is ICON-D2 with a 2 km step. Ensembles are downloaded at most once an hour so they don't burn mobile data.

So that the weighted mean doesn't lie, sources are counted by family: ICON-D2, ICON-EU and their ensembles are still one DWD model, so they are first averaged among themselves and enter the whole with one vote. Otherwise one institute would have several times the weight and "Source agreement" would report a certainty that isn't there.

Temperatures are corrected for the real height of the point from the DMR 5G elevation model: a model computes with the height of its grid, and when you are 200 m higher that alone is 1.3 °C of difference. For precipitation the median is taken instead of the mean (so a sharp shower doesn't smear into drizzle) and the rainiest variant is shown next to it — the rain warning is based on it too, so the risk doesn't hide. Model weights are computed separately for up to 6 hours ahead and beyond.

ČHMÚ is the only value on the screen that is not a forecast but an actual measurement from the nearest professional station (there are 758, so usually within a few kilometres) — temperature, humidity, pressure, wind, precipitation. It is also the yardstick for how well each model did. ČHMÚ publishes the data with roughly an hour's delay, so an older measurement gets a smaller weight in the overall estimate. Works only in Czechia and only when the company API is available (data is fetched through it — opendata.chmi.cz cannot be called directly from a browser).

With the arrow wheel at the top right you force the forecast anew at any time — everything is downloaded including ensembles and new radar images. Otherwise the weather refreshes itself every 15 minutes while the tool is open.

The When will it start raining card is the most accurate thing the app can do short-term: the first two hours don't come from a model but from radar (a DWD product, 1 km, 5-minute step) — radar sees the real precipitation field and just shifts it, so at this range it beats every model. Beyond that models continue at 15-minute steps so a twenty-minute shower doesn't get lost in an hourly average. The header says directly "Rain in 25 min", the bars below are intensity in mm/h (lighter = from a model, solid = from radar; hold to see time and value). Radar has limited coverage — in eastern Moravia the DWD grid no longer reaches and the card runs from models only, which it says itself. Radar can say "it's raining" but not by itself "it's not raining", so a dry forecast is always confirmed by models too.

Warnings about wind gusts come from ensembles, but not from their mean — the ninth decile (P90) is taken, i.e. the worst tenth of runs. A tripod with the instrument gets knocked over in that one bad scenario, not in the average of scenarios, and an average would smear such a gust away.

The precipitation radar shows animated how rain clouds move (~70 min back + 30 min outlook). The radar map can be panned and zoomed (+/− buttons and ⌖ back to your place), with the slider you play individual frames by hand. Pressure is converted to the site's altitude (sea level in brackets) and for rain the amount in mm is shown next to the probability.

  1. Without input it shows the weather at your position.
  2. With the pin icon you pick a place by tapping the map — the map stays controllable, so first pan and zoom to the job you're going to, then tap.
  3. In the field at the top you can also search for a place by name.

Alerts watch what hurts in the field: thunderstorm and rain within 3 h, wind above 8 m/s (tripod, range pole), frost and heat. The last downloaded forecast is remembered offline too.
slunce:
How much daylight is left and what to do with it in the field: sunrise, sunset, end of twilight, azimuth and elevation of the Sun, shadow length and the hours when the Sun will be in the line of sight.

  1. Until sunset remains… — from today's pace (how many points/h you measured today) it estimates how many more points you can still manage.
  2. Enter the height of a vertical (range pole, post) and you see the shadow length — usable for checking direction and for photo documentation.
  3. Enter (or take from the compass) the azimuth of the sight — the app lists the hours when the Sun will be low in that line and you won't see the display or the prism.

Everything is computed offline (NOAA, times ±1 min), azimuths to true north. The shadow is valid for level terrain. Checking the compass by the Sun is a separate button at the bottom.
dronview:
Opens the official air traffic restriction map of the Czech ANS (DronView) — no-fly zones, airport CTRs, restricted areas.

Before flying a drone on a job, check whether you may fly there and how high. Needs internet.
openKatastr:
Opens the cadastral map at your current position in the chosen source (Mapy.cz, iKatastr, ČÚZK Geoviewer — set in Settings → Map and points → Advanced).

Handy for quickly finding the parcel number and boundaries where you stand.

Details of any parcel without leaving the app: in the map switch on the Cadastral map layer (Layers button → Layers over the map) and tap inside a parcel. A card from RÚIAN opens — number, cadastral unit, municipality, official area and area from graphics (you see the difference at once), land type, use, boundary source (DKM to centimetres / UKM to metres), valid from, nearest address, terrain height from DMR 5G, possibly the building (house number, use, storeys, built-up and floor area, construction, year of completion) — and the parcel outline is highlighted. Below that Protection and restrictions from RÚIAN: BPEJ (decoded), national park / protected landscape area / reserve / monument and their buffer zones, Natura 2000, memorial tree, protected deposit area, mining area and the protection zone of a fundamental control point mark. Owner and title deed are returned by no free service; the "Owner and title deed" button opens this very parcel in the ČÚZK cadastre viewer (a captcha is required before owners there). Needs signal.
cadastre-vector:
Turns the cadastre into queryable data, not just a picture like WMS: parcel polygons from ČÚZK downloaded to the phone, so they work even without signal.

  1. On site download the parcels around you (needs internet once) — after that they stay offline in the job.
  2. The app tells you which parcel you stand on: number, area, land type and the distance to the nearest boundary.
  3. Boundaries are drawn in the map and in the AR camera.
  4. Navigate to the nearest boundary vertex saves it as a point and highlights it; you then look for the boundary stone by it.

Source: ČÚZK RÚIAN view service, layer Parcel (© ČÚZK). Cadastral boundaries have an accuracy given by their quality code — they are not a stake-out and in digitised maps they differ from reality by metres. As a fallback parcels can be loaded from a GeoJSON file.
cadastre-area:
Bulk import of ČÚZK control points: instead of searching point by point, drag to select a whole rectangle of territory and add the points in it at once.

  1. Open the tool and drag on the map to mark a rectangle.
  2. The app downloads the control points inside and offers to add them to the job.
  3. Confirm — the points then work offline, including AR and navigation.

Needs internet and the ČÚZK service being available; don't pick too large an area at once. Data © ČÚZK.
parcela:
Parcel geometry computed directly in plane S-JTSK coordinates (Gauss formula — the correct way to compute areas in Czechia) and land division to a given area.

  1. Build the polygon: by tapping the map, from job points, by entering Y and X, or by walking it with GPS.
  2. You get the area, perimeter and a boundary table — length and bearing of each side in gons and degrees.
  3. Division: parallel to a chosen edge, by a line from a chosen vertex, or into N equal parts. Enter the target area and the dividing line is computed.
  4. The computed vertices can be saved to the job and staked out right away.

The result is a field proposal, not a survey plan — that is done by a licensed surveyor. Division computes reliably for convex and ordinary irregular parcels.
project-import:
Loading a design into the field: a DXF drawing in S-JTSK (points, lines, polylines, texts, circles) is shown in the map and in the AR camera and you can stake out from it.

  1. Pick the DXF file. It copes with the positive surveying and the negative CAD coordinate notation.
  2. Switch individual drawing layers on and off so you don't look at everything at once in the field.
  3. At a vertex tap Stake out — it is saved as a job point and the app guides you to it with the arrow; or use Transfer all to job points.
  4. Instead of DXF you can also underlay a raster (a photo or scan of the site plan) — you georeference it with two points and it lies semi-transparent over the map.

The design is saved per job, so it is back after a restart. The drawing must be in S-JTSK — a drawing in a local system first seat with the Localization (Helmert) tool.
geo-overlay:
Your own plan under the map: a site plan, a survey plan, a scan of an old drawing or a base from the designer. After georeferencing you navigate by your own base, not just by ČÚZK.

  1. Pick an image (photo or scan).
  2. Mark control points: tap in the image and add the real coordinates to the point — S-JTSK Y/X by hand, from the current GPS, or by choosing an existing point.
  3. 2 points = similarity (Helmert) transformation: shift, rotation, scale. 3 and more = affine transformation by least squares; at each point you see the residual — a large residual means a badly hit point.
  4. Set the transparency; the base holds even with the map rotated.

The image is saved per job on the phone. No transformation straightens a scan of warped or crumpled paper — choose control points as far apart as possible and at the corners.
utility-networks:
"X-ray into the ground": utility lines (water, gas, electricity, sewer…) shown in the map and in AR under your feet, coloured by network type.

  1. Import the data from the network operator (DXF/GML from the utility statement).
  2. In AR you see the line routes projected onto the terrain, with depth if it is in the data.

Careful: the position of utilities in the documents tends to be approximate — before digging, the operator's stake-out always applies.
job-transfer:
Transferring a whole job between devices with an .argeo file (points, settings, sketches): send it to yourself by mail, messenger or via sharing.

  1. Send: pick the job → an .argeo file for sharing is created.
  2. Load: open the received file / pick it here — the job is added next to the existing ones (nothing is overwritten without confirmation).
hidden-points:
Overview of points hidden with the "Hide this point from AR" button. Tap Show to bring back a single point, or restore all at once.

Hiding lasts until the app restarts — after a fresh start the points are visible again.
brifink:
A morning briefing on one card: what awaits you in the field today, without clicking through four tools. It opens by itself at the first start of the day (switch off at the bottom of the card) or any time with this tile.

  1. Weather today: temperatures, when it should rain, wind, sunrise–sunset and how much daylight is left (offline it shows the last downloaded).
  2. GNSS today: from the stored satellite orbits it computes the best and worst window of the day (PDOP) + Kp index — during a geomagnetic storm GNSS misbehaves.
  3. Monitoring: points overdue for re-measurement.

The GNSS windows need downloaded orbits (the GNSS satellites tool) and a position; weather and Kp need internet for the first download.
checklist:
A morning packing list that builds itself: basics + equipment by the job's type of work + extra items by today's weather (frost → spare battery, rain → bag for the phone, heat → water, wind → weight for the tripod).

  1. In the morning open the tile and tick off what you have in the car.
  2. Add item saves your own things permanently (gate key…).
  3. Ticks apply to today and this job — tomorrow the list is clean again.

For weather items to be added, Weather must be downloaded. The type of work is set at the top of Tools in the "What are you doing today" strip.
bezpecnost:
A safety panel for working outside alone. At the top is the status: where I am (WGS84 and S-JTSK) and HOW OLD that position is, GPS accuracy, data connection, battery and who the position will be sent to.

  1. Emergency line 112 — the button must be held for 2 s and released (you see the countdown). Release earlier or off the button: nothing happens. It is a safeguard against an accidental touch in the pocket.
  2. 155 / 150 / 158 — the first tap only loads the number, the second one calls.
  3. Below that tiles: send position, SMS with position, copy, call a contact. Emergency contacts stay only on this phone.
  4. Today's risks (thunderstorm, heat, frost, wind, approaching darkness) fill in from the last downloaded weather and the twilight times. The switch turns on quiet reminders, "Mute for today" is one tap.

The app itself sends nothing anywhere and calls no one — it only opens the dialler, messages or sharing; whether the call went through or the SMS was sent it can't tell, so it doesn't claim it. On iPhone the battery is reported as unavailable (Safari doesn't provide it). The values at the risks are indicative recommendations, not quotes from regulations (Czech Gov. Reg. 361/2007). Reminders run only while the app is open.
kde-je:
With one tap you mark where your base, tripod, material or car is — and then it leads you there: distance, azimuth and an arrow turned by the compass.

  1. Before walking away from the car, tap Car (or Base / Tripod / Material / Custom).
  2. In the list you see the distance and arrow live — hold the phone in front of you as in AR.
  3. Show in map draws the markers into the main map; Clean up old deletes markers older than two days.

Markers aren't measured data: they aren't saved among job points nor into exports and reports. For base and tripod the fix accuracy is remembered — take it as the radius to search in.
zmenit-zakazku:
Switches the app to another job straight from Tools. Before, this was only possible on the start screen or in Settings → Job and data, so you had to click away from work in progress.

  1. The list shows the jobs you have access to — the open one has a tick and the point count.
  2. Tap to switch: the points, notes and settings of that job load and the map and AR are redrawn.
  3. + New job opens the same creation as on the start screen (including templates).

Work in progress isn't lost — it stays saved in the job you're leaving. In company mode permissions apply: whoever the admin assigned only some jobs sees and switches only those.
ucty-firma:
The company panel: who is signed in on this phone, what they may do and which company the phone belongs to. At the top a green strip with the company name, your name and role is always visible — and the Sign in / switch button.

  1. There are three roles: admin, management, employee. An employee uses the app normally in the field. Management can additionally get company overviews (Usage, Attendance). Admin can do everything: creates accounts, sets permissions, manages the company and sees the Overview.
  2. What you see in the panel depends on the role. Admin has the sections Overview, Users, Permissions, Usage, Attendance, Company and Help. Others have Companies and Help, plus Usage and Attendance if the admin allowed them.
  3. Several companies on one phone. The Companies section (admin has it inside the Company section) lists all companies you have ever signed in to: Switch, Forget and + Join another company (code). Switching always asks for a password or PIN. Points and jobs don't switch — they belong to the phone, not the company.
  4. Employees are added by the admin in the Users section. The colleague then enters the company code, name and password on their own phone — or at Invitation gets a QR shown and just types the password (the password is never in the QR).

Limited mode (the app without sign-in) can only do basic point measurement. Back to sign-in leads the strip at the bottom above the bar "Limited mode — Sign in", and also the button in this panel; so limited mode doesn't close for good.

When data doesn't download from the server, the section itself says WHY and what to do: no signal · this phone isn't signed in to the server · access expired · server error. Each message has a button (Try again or Sign in). An empty Attendance likewise says whether it is empty because nobody clocked in or because the data didn't download from the server.

Without the cloud the company lives only on this phone (transferred by an .argeofirma.json file). With the cloud, accounts, permissions, attendance and usage are shared among all the company's phones.
kniha-jizd:
A travel log tied to jobs: when, from where to where, how many kilometres and for which job. Monthly totals and CSV export for the accountant.

  1. Before leaving tap Leaving (you can enter the odometer), on arrival Arrived.
  2. Without an odometer the km are estimated from the straight-line distance ×1.3 — such trips are marked as estimates in the list.
  3. Enter by hand adds a trip retroactively, Export CSV saves the chosen month, Vehicle and rate sets the plate and CZK/km.

The app doesn't know statutory allowances or consumption — you enter the CZK/km rate and it is only a computation. Data is only on this phone and isn't part of the job backup, so export the CSV regularly.
moje-aktivita:
An overview of your own work: how long you had the app open, how far you walked and climbed, how many steps, how many points you added and which tool how many times and for how long you used. Plus a summary of the day and the last 7 days.

  1. Nothing to switch on — it counts by itself from app start (switch off with Measure my activity at the bottom of the window).
  2. The What I haven't touched section lists tools you never opened. The hide button hides their tile from Tools and from the list of actions — nothing is deleted, search still finds them and Hidden tools brings them back.
  3. Frequently used tools have a ☆ — it adds them to ★ Favourites at the top of Tools.
  4. Export CSV pulls out day by day for your own records.

The numbers are an overview, not a survey report: distance and elevation come from the phone's GPS (height is smoothed and only a step above 3 m counts), only walking is counted — above ~12 km/h nothing is added so that driving doesn't make kilometres. Steps are an estimate from the distance walked until you enable the accelerometer pedometer. Data stays on this phone and isn't part of the job backup.
predpisy: An offline cheat sheet from cadastral regulations: limit deviations, quality codes, deadlines and paragraphs. Curated content with the source stated; search by full text.
postupy:
A step-by-step cheat sheet for common methods: polar point, free station, tacheometry, traverse, technical levelling, GNSS-RTK…

Based on the official regulations (the cadastral renewal manual, the cadastral decree). For limits the source is always stated.
openDictModal: A surveying glossary of terms and abbreviations (TB, ZhB, Bpv, ZPMZ, GP…). Search in the field at the top; you can add your own terms at the bottom.
openCalcModal:
Surveying computations: bearing and distance from coordinates, polar point, intersection, angle conversions (°/gon), distance reduction into S-JTSK and more.

Enter coordinates in S-JTSK (positive Y, X). Results can be saved directly as a point.
agPosFromMap:
In a forest, a narrow street and between apartment blocks the phone's GPS is weakest — reflections off leaves and façades make errors of metres and averaging doesn't remove them. Yet you often see exactly where you stand: below you on the orthophoto is a house corner, a kerb, a manhole or a fork in the path. With this you read your position off the map and the app starts using it instead of GPS.

  1. Open Map and layers → Position from map. It offers to switch on the orthophoto — you recognise yourself best on it.
  2. Zoom the map in as far as possible (accuracy is computed from the scale) and tap exactly where you stand.
  3. The position marker turns amber, the accuracy circle becomes dashed and the Position from map tag hangs in the notifications. From then on AR arrows, distances, azimuths and "From GPS average" run from it.
  4. Cancel it with the Cancel tag or again with the same button (Back to GPS).

The accuracy doesn't lie: it comes from the map scale (metres per pixel × finger hit) and never goes below ±1 m — the orthophoto has its own error and your own stance can't be recognised better on it either. If the reading gives a worse number than GPS reports, the app says so and advises zooming in.

The manual position cancels itself once you walk more than 25 m away (recognised from the shift of raw GPS fixes — that shows walking reliably even when the absolute position is off) and doesn't survive a restart of the app. Both on purpose: a pinned position from another part of the job would be a trap.
bod-vypoctem:
A signpost for creating a new point from existing points — according to what you can measure:

  1. Polar point: you stand on a known point and have a direction + horizontal distance.
  2. Offset point: offset from a point by azimuth/bearing and distance.
  3. Forward intersection: you can't measure the distance — you intersect the point with sightings from two known stations.

The individual methods can also be found via search ("polar", "offset", "intersection").
err-log:
When something breaks in the app, the error is quietly written here — the app is written so that one broken tool doesn't bring down the rest, but then in the field there's no way to tell what actually failed. Here you find out.

  1. The list is from the newest: time, message and the place in the code where it crashed.
  2. Copy dumps the log as text — paste it into a bug report.
  3. Clear empties the list.

The last 40 records are kept, only on this phone; they survive a restart and are packed into the backup. A record in the log doesn't mean lost data — but the same error coming back is a trail worth sending.
gnss-signal:
A signpost of GPS quality: Satellites now (how many are above the horizon and what the geometry is), Signal prediction (skyplot with an obstruction mask — planning measurements by a forest or in built-up areas) and Site traffic light (score of reflections and stability at the current place).

Use it before a more precise measurement — wait for a better constellation or stand somewhere else.
pocasi-svetlo:
A signpost of everything the sky will do today — these used to be four separate tiles side by side:

  1. Weather: a forecast for the measuring site from up to 33 sources (in Czechia also the ČHMÚ ALADIN 1 km model and ČHMÚ measured data), the "when will it start raining" card from radar, precipitation radar, wind, pressure converted to your altitude.
  2. Sun and light: sunrise, sunset, end of twilight, shadow length and the hours when you'll have the Sun in the line of sight.
  3. GNSS forecast: when today's satellite geometry (PDOP) will be best and whether the ionosphere is misbehaving (Kp index).
  4. Today in the field: the morning briefing that sums all this up on one card.

The individual tools can still be found via search ("weather", "sun", "PDOP") — in the list of actions one row Weather and light stands for them.
prirucka: An offline cheat sheet for the field: Regulations & deviations (limit deviations, quality codes, deadlines — with the source stated), Measuring procedures (step by step: polar point, free station, levelling, GNSS-RTK…) and Glossary (terms and abbreviations).
overeni-bodu:
The spread of a measurement (σ in the Quality report) says how calm the measurement was — not whether the point is right. The GNSS error in a phone is systematically shifted during one session (atmosphere + momentary satellite geometry), so two hundred calm readings can be two hundred readings shifted half a metre the same way. The only check you can do with a phone is a second independent determination.

  1. Measure and save the point normally.
  2. Walk away and come back later — ideally after several hours or the next day, when a different set of satellites is above you.
  3. Open the point card and tap Check point. The app pre-fills the form (name K_…) and saves where you stand right now, with a link to the point being verified.
  4. You find the verdict here in Point verification — the point's row shows "Verified by second determination · Δ 12 cm (limit 39 cm)", or "Second determination OUTSIDE the limit".

When you use the Check measurement tool, the result is counted here by itself — this tool doesn't do its own check, it only reads what the app already knows.

There is no seal in the point card — it was removed on 31 Aug 2026. In practice only a fraction of points have a second determination (and a point saved a minute ago can't even have one), so under almost every point "Single determination — unverified" was lit and only got in the way. The deviation and verdict live here, where you ask for them yourself.

This tool shows all the job's points at once: which have a second determination within the limit, which are outside and which nobody verified. It can be exported to CSV as evidence.

The limit is the limit positional deviation 2·√2·mxy by the chosen quality code (Czech cadastral decree No. 357/2013, annex item 13) — the same values you find in the Handbook. The default is code 3 (new field survey, limit 39 cm).

What to watch out for: two determinations within 20 minutes of each other most likely have the same systematic error — they fit each other even if both are off. The app marks such a pair ⚠ and it counts less as a check. Points measured before this feature existed are paired by name ("K_B12" to "B12") and marked (by name).
protokol-vytyceni:
The paper you hand over: where the stake should have gone, where it really went and how far apart that is. The stake-out checklist used to remember only that a point is ticked — a list of what was to be staked out, not evidence of how it turned out.

  1. Stake out as before. When you stand at the point, tick it — in the Stake-out checklist or with the Staked ✓ button in the point card.
  2. At that moment the app also records the actual position where you stand. If GPS averaging is running, it takes the average — much better than one reading.
  3. Here you then find a table of ΔY, ΔX and positional deviation Δp with a verdict, and print it (or save as PDF) or export to CSV.

The limit is the limit positional deviation 2·√2·mxy by the chosen quality code (Czech cadastral decree No. 357/2013, annex item 13) — the same values as in the Handbook and in Point verification. The default is code 3, i.e. a 39 cm limit.

"Inconclusive" means the phone had worse accuracy at the tick than half the limit. Then "within the limit" would only say the error hid in the noise — so such a row gets no verdict. That's more honest than a green tick you can't rely on.

Points ticked before this feature existed have no actual position recorded — in the report they are "no position record". Just tick them again (untick and re-tick) next time you stand at them.
dvoji-mereni:
σ and ± at a point describe only the internal agreement of one occupation: the readings came within a few minutes from the same satellite constellation and with the same reflections. If the phone lies the same way the whole time, the readings fit beautifully and ± comes out small — and it has nothing to do with the truth.

The only honest number you get by measuring the same point a second time after a gap, when the satellites have moved. The difference Δ of the two determinations already contains the systematic part.

  1. Add a point to verify — pick a point you care about.
  2. In 25 minutes the app tells you the point is ready.
  3. Go back to it, let the averaged GPS settle and tap Measure again.
  4. You see Δ and its split into east and north and choose: keep the original, save the average of both, or overwrite with the new one.

From the difference ±Δ/√2 per single determination and ±Δ/2 for the average of both is estimated. It's an estimate from a single difference, so it is itself uncertain — but it is measured, not promised. The numbers are written into the Quality report.

A difference above ~3 m isn't noise but an error in one of the measurements (façade reflection, few satellites). Don't take the average there; measure a third time.
balicek-zakazky:
Downloads to the phone everything you need in the field without signal — but around the job, not around where you happen to stand. That's the whole difference from the older "Save for offline": that took the current GPS, so at home in the evening it downloaded the kitchen surroundings and on site there was nothing.

The centre is computed from the job points, so you can pack from anywhere — best in the office on Wi-Fi.

  1. Choose how large an area you want (the app advises by the job's extent).
  2. Pack — the ČÚZK control points, map, cadastral map, orthophoto and DEM terrain heights for the points are downloaded.
  3. At the end you see what worked and what didn't. An unfinished step can be run again.

Weather and the satellite forecast can't be pre-downloaded (they would go stale), so you find them only in the checklist with an Open button — for weather the app says whether the saved forecast is fresh and whether it is even from around the job.

Terrain heights are read only for points, not the whole area — the DEM has a cell of about ten metres and a square kilometre would mean tens of thousands of requests to ČÚZK. Data © ČÚZK.
oblasti-offline:
Downloads to the phone all official points (TB, ZhB, PPBP, levelling and gravity) of a whole district, region or the republic, plus an overview map. From then on the points around you come from the phone — they appear at once, without signal and without waiting for ČÚZK.

  1. At the top you see which district you're standing in — it is pre-selected.
  2. Choose District (a few MB, minutes), Region or Whole Czechia (~635,000 points, of the order of 100 MB, 10–25 minutes — do it on Wi-Fi).
  3. Tick points and/or map and tap Download. The download can be interrupted; progress is saved and the Continue button picks up.

Why the map only to overview level: detailed tiles (z17–18) would make over 100,000 pieces for a district and the OpenStreetMap server forbids bulk downloads. A detailed map of the place where you measure is downloaded by Save surroundings or Pack the job.

Packages on the phone can be Updated (ČÚZK occasionally adds or removes points) and Deleted — here and in Settings → Backup and maintenance → Free up space (there also the map downloaded by Save surroundings). Data © ČÚZK, map © OpenStreetMap contributors.
lovci-bodu:
Official points that you actually find in the field are saved into your collection. Nothing is sent anywhere; it's yours.

  1. Open an official point's card and walk to it — within 5 m, with GPS to 8 m, and stand for 15 s. The I found it button tells you what's still missing.
  2. Tap. The point gets a gold star in the map and score points by rarity in Czechia: TB 50 · ZhB 30 · levelling 10 · PPBP 3 · gravity 200.
  3. In Point hunters (Tools → Aids) you see the collection, how many of the district you're missing, awards (First stone, Triangle, Whole line, District, Summit…) and the Hunt tab — the nearest undiscovered points with a Take me there button and the Stone of the day for double.

How many points the district has and what you're missing the app can compute when the district is on the phone (Download area). On private land only with permission; gravity points tend to be in buildings.
bodove-pole:
A list of official control points (trig, densification, PPBP, levelling) sorted by distance from you — with azimuth, compass direction and S-JTSK coordinates. It answers a question the app couldn't before: which known point should I walk to to verify my position.

  1. Guide sets the point as the navigation target — you get an arrow and distance like for any other point.
  2. Anchor opens "GPS shift to a known point" with pre-filled coordinates. You stand on the point, let GPS settle and confirm — the app remembers how much GPS lies and subtracts it from newly measured points.

Filter at the top: TB + ZhB are the most precise (prefer them for the anchor), PBPP is denser but weaker. A levelling point is height only, no position anchor can be made from it — that's why its button is greyed out.

Works offline from downloaded points. With signal the Find nearby button fills in the surroundings. Data © ČÚZK.
gesta-zkratky:
Assign a tool you use all the time to a gesture and then launch it from memory — one stroke of the finger anywhere on the screen, without searching in Tools. The stroke has two parts and is drawn without lifting the finger: first the activation gesture (default ↓→), then straight after it the tool shortcut (e.g. ↑↓ = Weather).
