  1. + Add shortcut — pick a tool and draw its stroke. In the tool list you can type right away: it also searches by synonyms ("tape" finds distance measurement) and Enter confirms the first result.
  2. Try it — trainer: the app names a tool, you draw the gesture and it says whether it matches. Nothing is launched meanwhile.
  3. The activation gesture can be changed. It must have at least two strokes — one would be confused with panning the map.

Why an activation gesture and not the shortcut directly: the whole app surface is live (the map pans with the finger, in AR you walk over markers). If the shortcut were a single stroke, a tool would launch at every map pan.

A rule you can trip over: the shortcut must not start in the same direction the activation gesture ends in — two identical arrows in a row can't be drawn in one stroke. Settings refuses such an assignment.

A gesture doesn't start over buttons, fields, tiles, an open window or in the tool wheel — there a stroke means something else. It can also be switched on/off in Settings → Controls.
sprava-appky:
The app owner's console — not company administration. A company admin sees their own company; here you see all of them at once: how many people each has, when someone last measured in it and how much of the server's daily limit it used.

  1. Requests for more seats hang at the top. A company may have 10 people on its own; above that the admin sends a request with a reason and the cap is raised with one tap.
  2. Company row → expands the detail: seats, status, note, jobs, points, messages.
  3. Status: Running / Read only (measuring and downloading work, writing to the server doesn't) / Locked (nobody can sign in). Before you switch the app off for someone completely, "read only" throws nobody out mid-measurement.
  4. No activity for 90 days selects dead companies for bulk deletion; a single company is deleted only after typing its code.
  5. Message to all companies appears in the notifications of all users (e.g. a planned outage).

Opens in Settings → Account and app and only for whoever has the key saved (OWNER_KEY from the server — the same as for the feedback inbox). Without the key the server returns 403 — it decides about access, not a hidden button.
rocenka:
The year and month in numbers: how far you walked and climbed, how many points you measured, how many days you were in the field and which tool you used most. Plus a map of all points you measured in the year — every dot is one point, colour by month.

  1. Nothing to switch on and nothing extra is measured — the yearbook only reads what the app collects anyway.
  2. With the ‹ › arrows next to the year you switch to another year.
  3. At the bottom is What went well — badges. Only the earned ones show; no task list, no reminders, nothing for speed.

Why the first months are incomplete: the app keeps detailed daily activity (kilometres, steps, time) only 120 days back and has nowhere to get older data — so from its first opening the yearbook builds its own monthly archive that is never deleted. Points and the map are complete even retroactively, because points aren't deleted.

Everything stays on the phone. Nothing is sent anywhere and there's no leaderboard or comparison with colleagues.
kolize-bodu:
When two people work on a job, it easily happens that each takes the same corner from the other side. Then two points lie in the list a few decimetres apart, each under a different name — and nobody notices until the office.

  1. The app speaks up by itself after syncing with the colleague: "Two points lie almost on top of each other".
  2. In the window you see both names, when they were created and how much each accuracy can be trusted.
  3. You decide: the same point (average or keep mine), or two different points — then the app won't ask about this pair again.

Why the app doesn't decide by itself: two points 80 cm apart can be the same corner measured twice or two really different points (a building corner and the kerb next to it). Phone accuracy is exactly of this order, so nobody can tell from the numbers. Automatic merging would quietly delete honestly measured data.

Your colleague actually verified the point for you: when you confirm it's the same point, the second determination is used as a check measurement. Two independent determinations with a gap and from a different phone give an honest accuracy including the error the phone itself doesn't know about — and the point is promoted to the highest level of trust in the quality report.
sever-slunce:
Aligns north by the Sun. It is the only orientation in the app that needs no known point nearby.

When to use it: the compass in a phone is a magnetometer and near rebar, rails, cars or a switchboard it easily shows twenty degrees off — the AR arrow then points wrong and you may not notice. The other ways of aligning north (by a point, by intersection, on two points) need something known in sight. In the middle of a field, a meadow or a forest there is no such point. The Sun is always visible and its azimuth can be computed in advance to a tenth of a degree, offline.

  1. Choose how to aim. Aiming at the Sun — turn so that the rear camera points at the Sun (don't look into the Sun, you look at the display). Aiming along the shadow — stand with your back to the Sun and point the phone along your own shadow; the shadow points exactly opposite to the Sun, so it's the same measurement with no risk to the eyes.
  2. The arrow on the target and the number below say how many degrees and which way to turn still.
  3. When you're aiming, tap I'm aimed — measure and hold the direction for three seconds. The app doesn't take one instant but the median of all samples, so a slight hand tremor doesn't matter. The spread then shows how steadily you held.
  4. Tap Align north. The correction is stored exactly as when aligning north by a point and shows in AR at once. Just in case, there's Undo.

Accuracy: aiming a phone by hand works to about ±3–5°. That is an order better than a confused magnetometer, but it is no substitute for orientation on a known point — that's to tenths of a degree. Take it as a rescue where there's nothing to orient on.

The tool refuses to run when the Sun is higher than 65° above the horizon (around noon its azimuth changes fastest and aiming is least reliable) or when it is below the horizon. The Sun position computation is local (NOAA), works without signal.
odhadovacka:
An estimation training ground: first you guess, only then you learn the truth from real sensors. Three disciplines, one takes a few dozen seconds.

  1. Walk a distance — the app says e.g. "walk 38 m", you walk and tap I'm there. The truth is the distance walked from GPS. While walking it deliberately shows no metres, otherwise it wouldn't be a guess.
  2. Turn to an azimuth — you get an azimuth, turn and confirm. The truth is from the compass; it isn't shown during the discipline either.
  3. How far is it — the app picks a job point nearby, you estimate the distance by eye and type it. The truth is computed from GPS. This discipline needs a job with points within 500 m.

What it's for apart from fun: estimating distance and direction is a working skill. Whoever knows what thirty metres look like and where south-west is spots a silly mistake before saving it — swapped coordinates, a misread metre, a point in the next street. It is trained only by immediate feedback, and that you carry in your pocket anyway.

The score, the average of the last ten attempts and the best streak (how many attempts in a row scored 80 points or more) stay only on this phone; nothing is sent anywhere.

Honestly: mobile GPS has a metre-level error, so it is scored in per cent, not centimetres. The walking discipline refuses to run when GPS accuracy is worse than ±10 m — otherwise it would score noise, not your guess.
foto-protinani:
Determines a point you can't reach from two photos taken from two places. A building corner behind a fence, a roof element, a chimney, a point across the river.

How it differs from Forward intersection: the task is the same, but you don't have to aim the camera cross steadily at the target. At the station you just snap a photo (a second) and tap the target in the frozen image — with a finger, at leisure, even in the car. Also the target doesn't have to be in the middle of the frame, anywhere in the photo is enough.

  1. Switch on the camera (AR or split mode), stand so that you can see the target and photograph station A.
  2. Move at least 8 metres sideways — ideally so that you look at the target from another direction — and photograph station B.
  3. Tap the target on each photo. The red cross can be dragged with a finger until it fits exactly. Make sure you mark the same detail on both photos.
  4. The result is computed by itself. Tap Save as new point.

The most important thing in the whole tool — orientation. Forward intersection measures the difference of two sightings at each station, so a constant compass error cancels out. Here the azimuth is taken from the compass directly, so it doesn't cancel: ten degrees off means nine metres off at fifty metres. That's why at each photo you can pick a known point that is also visible on it and tap it too (blue cross). The target's azimuth is then computed from that point's true azimuth and the compass error drops out of the result. Without orientation the tool still computes, but marks the result as approximate and includes the compass error in the accuracy estimate.

What to watch out for: mind the intersection angle — below 12° the rays are almost parallel and the position is uncertain; moving farther sideways helps. The accuracy of the result also depends on the GPS of both stations, which isn't included in it. The stated height is above eye level at the station (holding height from Settings), not above sea level.
plakat-dne:
The day you've just had as one picture: the track you walked drawn as a line, points measured that day as dots and four big numbers — how many points, how many kilometres, how much time in the field and how many metres of climb. It can be sent to a group or attached to the site diary.

  1. Open the tile — the poster for today draws itself; at the top switch to yesterday or any date.
  2. Share sends the finished PNG via system sharing (WhatsApp, mail, Photos).
  3. Save image downloads it to the phone. On an older iPhone it opens in a new tab instead — hold a finger on it and save to Photos.

The same Poster button is also at the bottom of the Day journal and takes over the day you have chosen there. The journal is text for the office, the poster is a picture — two forms of the same day.

Honestly: distance walked and metres of climb come from mobile GPS, so they are approximate. The poster is not survey evidence; that's what reports are for. It works offline and sends nothing anywhere — the picture is made right on the phone.
prohlidka:
A mode for looking around, not for work. You raise the phone and the app answers a single question: where you stand and what is around. It creates no job, saves no points and measures nothing — it can be run even without sign-in, at the weekend or from a window when you want to show someone where the property boundary runs.

  1. Open the tile. At the bottom a panel appears with the parcel under your feet (number, land type, area, cadastral unit), the distance to the nearest boundary, altitude and Sun position.
  2. Show in camera switches to the camera — over parcel areas labels with their number and area appear and faintly their boundaries too.
  3. The panel can be collapsed with the arrow so you see the whole image. The cross ends the walk-through.

The surroundings are downloaded to 350 m and kept on the phone, so after a while it works without signal too; once you walk more than 200 m, new surroundings are fetched.

Honestly: "you stand on parcel X" is only as reliable as the phone's position. When a boundary is closer than the reported GPS accuracy, the app stops claiming certainty and says you're on the boundary of two parcels — the neighbour is equally likely. Data © ČÚZK (RÚIAN).
trenazer:
Dry-run practice. The app scatters practice points and sends you to stake them out; at the end it tells you how many centimetres off you were and how long it took. A newcomer learns without messing up a real job — and outside work it's a game.

Two disciplines. Staking out points — five points, at each you see distance and azimuth. Finding a point — no numbers, only "hot / close / far", like searching for an overgrown boundary stone in the field.

Two modes depending on where you are.

  • Outdoors (1 : 1) — the position is real from GPS, the points are 10–60 m around you and you really walk to them.
  • At home — you don't have to be outside. The position is fictional and you move by holding the "Go" button: you go where the phone points. Compass and camera are real meanwhile, so you turn in the room and search — and you practise exactly what you do outside: reading the arrow, not overshooting, walking up and adjusting.

How accurate the GPS is sets the simulated noise (0 / ±1 / ±3 m). A point that fits on the display then may not fit on the ground — and that's the most important thing one learns in the field. The deviation is computed from the truth, not from what you see, so blind trust in the arrow shows in the result.

Nothing mixes into work: the trainer saves not a single point, touches neither the job nor exports, and the fictional position stays inside the trainer — it doesn't get into measurement, averaging or reports. After closing or restarting the app nothing remains but your best result. While it runs a strip at the top says the position isn't real.
vektor-mapa:
A map base drawn, not downloaded as an image. You pack an area in advance and have it in the field without signal — sharp at every zoom, because it is drawn (buildings, roads and paths, water, rails, forest and meadows).

  1. It can be packed from the office. Pan and zoom the map to where you're going — no GPS needed — and tap Pack this extent. The panel shows how big the extent is; the cap is 12 km².
  2. The Draw vector map into the base checkbox switches the layer on above the normal tiles. It stays on after an app restart.
  3. Mute colours is for direct sun and for night.
  4. You can have several packed areas and switch between them; the cross deletes one you no longer need.

A town with surroundings comes to a few MB instead of the hundreds raster tiles would take.

Honestly: it's a base for orientation, not a survey base. The data is from OpenStreetMap (© OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL) — volunteer-made, no positional guarantee; a building in it can be metres off. Don't read coordinates off it and don't confuse it with the cadastre or the orthophoto.
zapis-dne:
A signpost to two records that are made in the evening — these used to be two separate tiles:

  1. Day journal: what you did today, on which job and for how long — a written record for the timesheet.
  2. Poster of the day: the same day as one picture (track map, numbers, weather) to send to the group.

Both items can still be found via search ("journal", "poster").
moje-cisla:
A signpost to your own numbers — none of it is measurement and none of it goes into job points:

  1. My activity: how far you walked, how many metres of climb, which tools you use — and what to hide from Tools.
  2. Yearbook: the year and month in numbers, a map of places you've been, badges and streaks.

Both items can still be found via search ("activity", "yearbook").
podklady-katastr:
A signpost to the bases you pull into the map and into AR. Cadastre where I stand right now stays a separate tile — that's one tap and the most frequent thing.

  1. Look around: what is around me — boundaries, neighbouring parcels, without creating a job.
  2. Parcels into the map and AR: vector boundaries from the cadastre; can be staked out and exported.
  3. Download points from the map extent: control points from the area you have on screen.
  4. Offline vector map: an OSM extent packed in the office, draws even without signal.
  5. Pack the job for the field: map, cadastre and points around the JOB, not around you — done on Wi-Fi before leaving.

The first three need signal. All items can still be found via search ("parcels", "offline", "pack").
srovnat-sever:
A signpost for the situation "the markers in AR don't fit reality". The verb "Align AR" had ten rows in the tools and all promised the same — here each option says WHAT is wrong. Three separate tiles stay at the top: Seat AR (guide) when you don't know where to start, Compass when you just want to look, and Align north — the most common one.

First decide a single thing: is everything rotated, or shifted sideways? Choose accordingly:

  1. Align on two points — the markers are shifted AND rotated. You aim at two known points and north and position are aligned at once. Most precise when you have two points in different directions (not in line).
  2. Align north by a point — the position fits but everything is rotated. You aim at ONE known point and the azimuth is corrected; the position is untouched.
  3. Align north by the Sun — the compass lies (rebar, fence, car, switchboard) and there's nothing to aim at. North is computed from the Sun's position and time. Needs a view of the sky.
  4. Correct GPS shift by a point — the rotation fits but everything is shifted the same way. You stand on a known point and the position is corrected; north is untouched.
  5. Localization (Helmert) — the design isn't in S-JTSK but in a local system (site grid). From two or more identical points a transformation key for the whole job is computed.
  6. Measure the camera field of view — markers fit in the middle of the image but drift at the edges. The real field of view of this phone is measured; done once and valid from then on.

⚠ Azimuth correction and position correction are two different things. If you reach for the wrong one, the markers line up where you stand and a bit farther they'll be worse than before. When unsure, take Align on two points — it solves both at once.

All options can still be found via search ("helmert", "sun", "fov", "markers don't fit"). Every correction can be cancelled in the Compass.
ar-dosah:
AR normally shows only points within the set range (Settings → Frequent → Visibility of points in the AR camera, usually 100 m). With this tool you pick points you want to see even from afar — e.g. a base two kilometres away.

  1. Start the tool. If you're in the pure camera, the app switches to split view — selection is done in the map.
  2. Move the map to that area with two fingers (pan and zoom) — you don't have to be there.
  3. Select a rectangle: either drag it with one finger, or tap one corner and then the opposite one (between taps you can keep panning the map). Points inside are added to the selection and for the extent the app fetches the control points from ČÚZK, even if it has never been there. You can make several extents in a row.
  4. Done. Selected points have a blue outline in AR and show regardless of range — in the map too, even kilometres from you. The selection survives closing the app and is kept separately per job.
  5. Cancel with the Clear selection button next time you start the tool.

At most 400 points can be selected. That's not stinginess: the range is also a performance cut thanks to which AR doesn't go through the whole ČÚZK control point set on every frame. Mind the accuracy too — a marker two kilometres away shifts by more than a hundred metres with a 3° compass error, so it's an indicative direction, not a stake-out.
zdravi-appky:
One screen that says whether the phone gives the app everything it needs: version and offline layer, GPS, compass, camera, storage, account and the latest errors. Green = fine, amber = worth a look, red = this slows the app down.

When something doesn't work, tap Send to the author — the overview is put into the message and you add what was happening. The compass is measured for two seconds; on iPhone it wakes up only after the first touch on the screen.
chybovy-rozpocet:
How far the point can really be from the marker you see in AR — broken down by error source.

  1. GPS gives the position with ±σ (from the chip, or the standard error of the average from Precise GPS).
  2. Compass gives the direction with ±σc; at distance d that makes d·sin σc across — the direction error grows with distance.
  3. Both add under the square root (law of error propagation): σpoint = √(σGPS² + σacross²).

Try "what if" with the sliders: north alignment by a point (±1°), getting within 10 m, averaged GPS. The From sensors button restores the real values. It is ±1σ — in one case out of three the point is even farther.
cvicne-ulohy:
22 exercises with a known result: bearing and distance, polar point, orthogonal method, intersection from angles and from distances, traverse, levelling.

  1. Pick an exercise and compute it — by hand, or with the Open in Calculator with data button (the input is pre-filled; the Calculator also shows the procedure).
  2. Enter the result and tap Check. The app says "correct", or by how much and in which direction it's off.
  3. After two failed attempts the solution can be shown.

Coordinates are in S-JTSK (positive Y, X), angles in gons, left-hand vertex angles. Progress stores only which exercises you have done.
poznavacka:
A quiz on monuments and marks in the field: trig point, witness point, levelling bolt and stone, survey nail, boundary stone, pipe, stake, building corner, tower.

Each has a sketch and description; choose from four options. After answering you learn what the point is for, how to recognise it and what it gets confused with, with a link to the Glossary and to the nearest real point (Control points). Order and options are shuffled; only the best result is remembered.
vzorce:
A formula cheat sheet: coordinate computations (bearing, polar point, orthogonal, intersection, Helmert), traverse, heights (levelling, trigonometric height difference), distances (tape, reduction, Křovák), accuracy (mean, error propagation, limit deviations), angles and conversions.

Each formula has the meaning of the symbols and a link to where the app computes it. Numeric limits (limit deviations) are in Handbook → Regulations and deviations. Search at the top.
pohled-3d:
A separate map from an oblique bird's-eye view: buildings extruded to height (from OpenStreetMap; where the height is missing, an 8 m estimate), terrain from elevation tiles, above it the job points, the loaded DXF drawing (axis thick) and your position. Two fingers = rotate and tilt; buttons On me, North, 2D / 3D and Terrain.

What for: when staking out corners and edges you verify you stand at the right one, and with profiles you see cut and fill before digging. Tapping a building tells the height and house number, tapping a drawing line the axis chainage. Tapping a point slides out the classic point card over the 3D view (3D stays open) and a small bar with Navigate stays at the bottom — the same navigation as from the map, the terrain route is drawn here too and after closing it keeps running in split and in AR.

Pavements: pavements, paths, crossings and stairs from map data as strips at real width (1.8 m pavement, 2.5 m crossing, 3.5 m pedestrian zone) with a dark kerb on both sides, laid on the terrain — you can tell whether a point lies on the pavement or in the road (the width is an estimate from the map). Greenery: forest and scrub as semi-transparent volumes. Points at height: a point with a height gets a post from the ČÚZK DMR 5G terrain (a levelling mark in a wall, a point on a bridge); below 0.4 m it isn't drawn. Zooming out (from a view of the whole of Czechia) the map curls into a globe — it's the real Earth, not exaggerated curvature.

Needs the vector map switched on (Layers → Base map → Map) and WebGL — in weaker-phone mode it isn't offered. Terrain downloads extra tiles (~40 kB each); without signal it can be switched off with the Terrain button.
scroll-uceni:
Geo cards — cards to swipe through — one screen = one thing, thumb up for the next. They are built from what the app has: terms from the glossary, formulas (the Compute button opens the Calculator), regulations (deviations, quality codes…), questions from the exercises (tap to reveal the result), what the app can do (Open launches the tool) and tips from the field.

At the top a filter by kind and ★ Saved; the star on a card saves it. Unseen cards go first, the order is shuffled every day; the counter shows how many you went through today.
mistopisny-nacrt:
A sketch for the selected point (open the point card or navigate to it, then start the tool). Base: Paper = a white sheet with rough outlines from the vector map (buildings, roads, paths, water, rails, forest), Map = raster, Orthophoto. What you draw on one you see on the others too — the sketch is in coordinates.

Distance: tap from and to — the dimension has the length from coordinates; tapping it you enter the value measured with a tape (then bold in the sketch). It snaps to points, building corners and objects. Object: tree, bush, post, manhole, hydrant, stone, sign — tap where it belongs. Line: a fence or edge by tapping, Done finishes. Text anywhere. Delete by tapping an element, Undo takes back the last step. Trees from the orthophoto = an estimate: from the ČÚZK orthophoto extent dark or textured green patches (crowns) are taken and added as trees with a dashed edge — accuracy ~2–3 m, it confuses hedges and flower beds; delete what doesn't fit.

PNG makes a paper version with north arrow, scale bar and legend and offers sharing. The sketch is saved with the point in the job.
korekce-z-mapy:
Simply: the phone's GPS is off by a few metres, but for a while always in the same direction. On the orthophoto you see exactly where you stand — to half a metre. You tap there, the app computes how much GPS is off right now and subtracts that while walking too: in AR, in navigation, in distances and in the points you save. The static "Position from map" (I stand still, GPS isn't used) stays separate — this one is for walking.

  1. Stand 30–60 s in an open spot (not under a tree, not by a wall) so GPS averages — the window shows how many readings there are already.
  2. Switch the map to orthophoto, zoom in as far as possible (zoom 20+, a tap is then ±0.5–0.8 m) and tap Tap where I stand → tap exactly your spot (building corner, kerb, manhole).
  3. The app shows how much and where GPS is off and the accuracy of the correction (tap ⊕ GPS average). Switch on — valid for 10 min / 100 m from the tap spot; the pill at the top counts down and tells you when to tap again. Leave the "shift the live position too" checkbox on (without it only saved points are corrected, as with the other corrections).

What to expect: from ±3–5 m to ±1.5–2 m for a few minutes. From one fix without standing still the correction is rather random (4 m → 3 m) — the app says so. Under trees and between houses the GPS error changes every few metres; there it won't help. Points saved with this correction have the origin "map tap" in the card; they aren't shifted a second time (the fixes are already shifted).
kvalita-gps-mapa:
Computes around you (220 × 220 m) how much sky is visible from each 4 × 4 m cell: from building and forest heights in the vector map, 16 directions, up to 60 m. Green = open sky, amber = half the sky (measure longer, average), red = by a wall or between houses (move, or use the step offset). The layer stays in the map; hide it in the Layers panel → "GPS quality".

It's an estimate from shading, not a measurement: it doesn't see trees outside forests, cars or reflections off glass. The surroundings watcher and the accuracy silhouette watch the actual reception — this tells you in advance where it's worth going. Needs the vector map switched on (Layers → Base map → Map).
nacrt-na-mapu:
The phone leads you to an official point to ±3–5 m — beyond that GPS says nothing. The ČÚZK site sketch does, when laid on the cadastre: which side of the fence, post or corner the point is on.

  1. In the map open the card of an official point (TB, ZhB, PPBP, levelling). Below the official sketch tap Lay the sketch on the map.
  2. Tap the point mark in the sketch — the app knows its coordinates, so the first control point is done.
  3. Tap in the sketch a building corner or boundary vertex that you also find in the map, and then the same corner in the map. A tap within 3 m snaps to a cadastral vertex (downloaded parcels, otherwise live RÚIAN).
  4. The sketch is stretched and rotated onto the map (shift + rotation + scale). With the bar at the bottom you set the transparency, switch on display in AR (the sketch is projected on the ground around the point) or add another corner — from three pairs it's an affine transformation and the bar says how much the points disagree.

Honestly: sketches tend to be schematic, not to scale → the surroundings fit to ±0.5–1 m. It's good for "which side", not for "where to dig" — for that there are the tie distances from the sketch and a tape. The point itself is always exactly on its coordinates in the image. A corner from DKM is centimetres, a corner from UKM (converted analogue map) ±1 m, a corner without cadastre has the accuracy of your tap. One sketch at a time; the placement is remembered for a month.
opravit-gps:
A signpost for the situation "GPS drifts by a few metres" — the position on the map and the markers in AR are shifted, but the rotation is right. Three ways, depending on what you have at hand:

  • Walking along an edge — walk a kerb, the boundary of a plot or an edge from the drawing; the app compares the track with the edge and computes the offset (also retroactively for points measured before).
  • From the map while walking — tap in the orthophoto or the map where you are standing right now; it also shifts the live position, valid for 10 minutes / 100 m.
  • From a known point — stand on an official point (TB, ZhB, PPBP, levelling) and let the offset be computed from its coordinates; corrects position and height.

The offset concerns position, not north — rotated markers are fixed by Align north.
dva-telefony:
A signpost for the tools that need a second phone:

  • Two-phone DGPS — one phone stands on a known point as a base and sends corrections, the other (rover) receives them; a temporary base from Precise GPS works too.
  • Acoustic rangefinder — the distance between two phones to centimetres from a sound chirp; from several distances a point can be intersected.

Both phones need QTRIG and a connection (network or QR).
